newsitem.title: USA: Cookware, games, exercise video for kids.
newsitem.headline: Cookware, games, exercise video for kids.

text.p: T-Fal, maker of non-stick cookware, has introduced a line of electric deep fryers with non-stick interiors designed to free the tentative chef of "fear of frying."

Frying should not be a dirty word, T-Fal says, because when the oil is at the correct high temperature, food is immediately sealed on the outside, absorbing less oil than if cooked in lower-temperature oil.
The new Superclean line has fryers in 1.5 pound to 2.2 pound capacities, with locking lids to prevent splattering and thermal construction to ensure that the exterior is always cool to the touch.
The line of fryers also is engineered to absorb unpleasant frying odours, the Pine Brook, N.J.-based company says.
The Supercleans range in price from about $50 to $90, depending on size and features. For more information, T-Fal can be contacted by calling 201-575-1060.
As the Milton Bradley game Twister celebrates its 30th anniversary and Yahtzee celebrates its 40th, the games maker is introducing a new game, Last Chance.
This game, aimed at adults, is a dice game in which players bid for the opportunity to play a card that features a certain poker combination depicted by dice chips.
Last Chance rules allow a player to bet all his or her money for the rights to a card. The player with all the cards wins.
The game sells for about $20. For more information, call Milton Bradley at its East Longmeadow, Mass., headquarters at 413-525-6411.
In honour of its favourite pests, d-Con, maker of rodenticides and pesticides, has designated October as National Rodent Prevention Month.

An estimated 21 million homes are invaded by rodents each year, d-Con says. It is especially noticable in mid-October, when the weather begins to get colder and rain and snow disrupt rodents' outdoor food supplies.
For a free brochure on spotting, controlling and preventing rodent infestation, write to d-Con Consumer Brochure, P.O. Box 8737, Young America, Minn. 55551.
For a free brochure on hantavirus, a rodent-borne virus that can cause serious illness in humans, call the hantavirus helpline at 1-800-395-3266.
Here's a new exercise video with a twist -- it's aimed at pre-teens, specifically the couch potato variety.

"No More Couch Potato Kids: Strength and Shape" is a 40-minute exercise video developed by Pat Lawrence, a mother and founder of the video's distributor, Earth Smart Inc., with the guidance of Stu Kaminsky, a personal trainer and expert in adolescent exercise and motivation.
The video is a product of a personal experience.
"There's nothing more difficult for a mother to watch than her child grow up overweight and self-conscious ... I couldn't watch my son do that. This video was my way of reaching out," said Lawrence.
"No More Couch Potato..." concentrates on flexibility and strength. Its primary goal is to instill self-confidence, while emphasising the enjoyment of exercise.
"There is no pressure of someone watching the kid's every move. It's (the video) just about developing a love for fitness that will last a lifetime," said Lawrence.
The video costs $14.95 and can be ordered by writing Earth Smart Inc., PO Box 115, Lincroft, N.J. 07738-0115. Or call 1-800-EXERCI-4 (393-7244).
Not too long ago I wrote about the book, "Polish Your Furniture with Panty Hose," in which author Joey Green offered some unusual new ways to use traditional products.
Green has published a second book, "Paint Your House with Powdered Milk," containing hundreds of "offbeat uses for brand-name products."

Suggestions include making modelling clay or glue from Gold Medal flour, removing candle wax with Coppertone sun tan products, preventing a car door from freezing shut with Pam cooking spray, and preventing cats from scratching woodwork with Tabasco pepper sauce.

The title refers to the use of milk paint by early American colonists. Today, you can mix Carnation non-fat dry milk with water until it is the consistency of paint. Add water-based colour for the desired hue.
The book, published by Hyperion, costs $7.95 in the United States and $10.95 in Canada. It is due in bookstores in mid-October.
